papers.title_in_file: Quantum State Preparation via Neural Network Encoding in Quantum Machine Learning
papers.version_note: arXiv:2605.31006v1 [quant-ph], 29 May 2026; the text layer holds one copy of the paper.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that trains a CNN to map an image to the parameters of a fixed quantum circuit that prepares its FRQI state, tested on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at 32 × 32 pixels with 11 qubits, and compared in runtime with per-image MPS sweeping optimization.

existing.note: Value is right. The paper also names the baseline: an MPS circuit (D=6, chi_max=256) optimized per image with the sweeping procedure of Ref. [20]; the 3.27 s is a mean over 10 samples, with substantial variance across samples.
existing.value: The authors report that the baseline, an MPS circuit (D=6, χmax=256) optimized for each test image individually with the iterative sweeping procedure of Ref. [20], requires 3.27 s per image averaged over 10 samples, terminating early once a fidelity of F ≥ 0.950 is reached.
quotes: As a baseline, we optimize an MPS circuit (D=6, χmax=256) for each test image individually using the iterative sweeping procedure of Ref. [20], terminating early once a fidelity of F ≥ 0.950 is reached.
Averaged over 10 samples, the baseline requires 3.27 s per image
existing.certainty_reason: Started LOW: an empirical result from one study.
existing.reader_inference: The 3.27 s is a mean over only 10 samples, while the encoder latency (0.497 ms) is reported as a median; the two statistics differ.

existing.note: The two headline figures come from different configurations. 0.992 is the FRQI ansatz at D=8 on Fashion-MNIST (0.981 on MNIST); the speedup is measured for the center-sequential ansatz at D=6 targeting F ≥ 0.950 against per-image MPS sweeping, as a median latency of 0.497 ms and a ∼ 6580-fold speedup. The abstract's 'more than 5000-fold' is below the body's 6580-fold figure.
existing.value: The authors report fidelities up to 0.992 on unseen images (the FRQI-native ansatz at D=8 on Fashion-MNIST; 0.981 on MNIST) and a per-data-instance runtime reduction of more than 5000-fold in the abstract; in the runtime analysis the speedup is a median prediction latency of 0.497 ms per image, a ∼ 6580-fold speedup over per-image optimization, for the center-sequential ansatz at depth D=6 targeting F ≥ 0.950.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the FRQI representation the address qubits encode the pixel position and a single color qubit encodes the grayscale intensity in the interval from 0 to 1, so that an image with two to the power A pixels is represented using n = A + 1 qubits.

n = A + 1 qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: FRQI is attributed to Refs. [22, 23]; the paper restates it as the representation it uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that they adopt hierarchical (Morton, Z-order) pixel indexing, in which the two most significant bits of the pixel index identify the image quadrant, the next two identify the sub-quadrant, and so on recursively.
quotes: the two mostsignificant bits of j identify the image quadrant, the next two identify the sub-quadrant, and so on recursively
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.a states the indexing used in the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hierarchical (Z-order) ordering has been shown to achieve lower entanglement entropies, citing earlier work.
quotes: This ordering has been shown to achieve lower entanglement entropies [12, 20].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Refs. [12, 20]; this paper does not test row-based against Z-order.

assertions.value: The authors state that the encoder consists of three successive Conv–Swish–MaxPool blocks with 32, 64, and 128 filters (3 × 3 kernels), mapping a 32 × 32 grayscale image to a 4 × 4 × 128 feature map that is flattened to a 2048-dimensional vector, followed by a three-layer MLP with 256 hidden units and Swish activations, giving a backbone of approximately 749,000 trainable weights independent of the ansatz.
quotes: The encoder consists of three successive Conv–Swish–MaxPool blocks with 32, 64, and 128 filters (3 × 3 kernels), transforming a 32 × 32 grayscale image to a 4 × 4 × 128 feature map before flattening to a 2048-dimensional vector.
A three-layer MLP with 256 hidden units and Swish activations follows, giving a backbone of approximately 749,000 trainable weights independent of the ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the encoder it uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the bounded variant a sigmoid nonlinearity constrains each encoder output to the interval from 0 up to, but not including, 2π, and that the final linear projection is initialized with small variance scaling to prevent large initial rotation angles.
quotes: A final linear projection maps to θ, initialized with small variance scaling to prevent large initial rotation angles.

assertions.value: The authors state that the center-sequential circuit has Nparams = 4(n − 1)D + n parameters, which for n = 11 qubits at depth D = 6 is Nparams = 251.
quotes: This yields a parameter count of Nparams = 4(n − 1)D + n. For n = 11 qubits at depth D = 6, this translates to Nparams = 251.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A states the ansatz's parameter count.

assertions.value: The authors state that the FRQI-native ansatz starts from Hadamard gates giving a uniform superposition and applies layers of two parts, first entangling the address qubits through nearest-neighbor (N2) and next-nearest-neighbor (N3) gates, then applying Ry rotations controlled by the address qubits, and that it has Nparams = (9n − 21)D parameters, which for n = 11 qubits at depth D = 6 is Nparams = 468.
quotes: After initializing the qubits in a uniform superposition via Hadamard gates, it applies layers that consist of two parts.
First, the address qubits are entangled via nearest-neighbor (N2) and next-nearest-neighbor (N3) gates. Second, the Ry rotations controlled by the address qubits are applied.
For D layers, this yields a parameter count of Nparams = (9n − 21)D. For n = 11 qubits at depth D = 6, this gives Nparams = 468.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A states the ansatz and its parameter count.
assertions.reader_inference: The Table I counts for the other depths (156, 312, 624) agree with this formula.

the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10−3 on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluate MNIST and Fashion-MNIST with both circuit architectures at circuit depths D ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8}, and that Table I reports all configurations after 100 training epochs on 2048 held-out samples.
quotes: using both circuit architectures and circuit depths D ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8} in terms of quality and speed.
Table I presents the fidelity, PSNR, and SSIM of all configurations after 100 training epochs, evaluated on 2048 held-out samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV states the evaluation grid.

assertions.value: The authors report that all configurations converge within the first ∼20 epochs, with the strongest gain between D=2 and D=4, and that beyond D=6 improvements plateau: the FRQI ansatz improves from a fidelity of 0.972 to 0.981 on MNIST, and the center-sequential ansatz from 0.946 to 0.952.
quotes: All configurations converge within the first ∼20 epochs, with the strongest performance gain occurring between D=2 and D=4.
Beyond D=6, improvements plateau: the FRQI ansatz improves from a fidelity of 0.972 to 0.981 on MNIST, while the center-sequential ansatz only increases marginally from 0.946 to 0.952.
assertions.reader_inference: The 0.972 to 0.981 step (D=6 to D=8) is 0.009, comparable to the ± 0.011 to 0.012 reported in Table I.

assertions.value: The authors report that both circuit architectures exhibit training instability at higher depths, more pronounced for the FRQI ansatz at D ∈ {6, 8}, which they relate to its larger parameter count (468–624 versus 251–331 for center-sequential).
quotes: Both circuit architectures exhibit training instability at higher depths, though this effect is more pronounced for the FRQI ansatz at D ∈ {6, 8}, consistent with the larger parameter count of this architecture (468–624 versus 251–331 for centersequential).
assertions.reader_inference: The Fig. 4 curves are not in the text layer, so the size of the instability cannot be checked.

assertions.value: The authors report that the FRQI ansatz outperforms the center-sequential ansatz at every depth on both datasets.

quotes: The FRQI ansatz outperforms the center-sequential ansatz at every depth on both datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I fidelities agree: at each depth the FRQI value exceeds the center-sequential value on both datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that at comparable parameter budgets the FRQI ansatz achieves higher fidelity: FRQI at D=4 with 312 parameters reaches a fidelity of 0.960 on MNIST, surpassing center-sequential at D=8 with 331 parameters and fidelity of 0.952.
quotes: At comparable parameter budgets, FRQI consistently achieves higher fidelity: for example, FRQI at D=4 with 312 parameters reaches a fidelity of 0.960 on MNIST, surpassing center-sequential at D=8 with 331 parameters and fidelity of 0.952.
assertions.reader_inference: The worked example compares 312 with 331 parameters, so the budgets are close but not equal; the shaded percentile bands of Fig. 5 are not in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that, at matched parameter counts, FRQI consistently achieves higher fidelity, confirming that the gain is architectural rather than a consequence of increased model capacity, and in the conclusion that the FRQI-native circuit achieves higher fidelity per parameter than the center-sequential architecture.
assertions.anchor: Fig. 5 caption, p.5; Section V, p.6
quotes: At matched parameter counts, FRQI consistently achieves higher fidelity, confirming that the gain is architectural rather than a consequence of increased model capacity.
The comparison between ansatz families further shows that the FRQI-native circuit achieves higher fidelity per parameter than the center-sequential architecture
assertions.reader_inference: The evidence is the comparison of depth sweeps for two ansatz families on two datasets; the paper runs no control that varies parameter count with the ansatz structure held fixed.

assertions.value: The authors report that Fashion-MNIST achieves higher fidelity than MNIST at every configuration (for example 0.986 versus 0.972 for FRQI at D=6).

assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no test of this explanation.

assertions.value: The authors state that higher fidelity does not necessarily imply better visual reconstruction, and that Fashion-MNIST yields lower PSNR and SSIM because its images contain high-frequency textures such as textile patterns and structured details, which the model smooths while preserving overall shape and class identity.

assertions.value: The authors state that the runtime comparison is the wall-clock cost of state preparation against per-image classical optimization on the same hardware (CPU inference).

assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no training time for the encoder, so the one-off cost of the offline phase is not in the speedup figures.

assertions.value: The authors state that their method uses the MPS-inspired center-sequential ansatz targeting the same fidelity threshold as the baseline, and that matching F ensures a fair comparison at equivalent preparation quality even though the two circuit architectures differ in structure.
quotes: Our method uses the MPSinspired center-sequential ansatz targeting the same fidelity threshold; although the two circuit architectures differ in structure, matching F ensures a fair comparison at equivalent preparation quality.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists a mean fidelity of 0.946 ± 0.018 on MNIST for center-sequential at D=6, below the 0.950 threshold, and the text does not report the encoder's fidelity on the 10 timed samples.

assertions.value: The authors report that the baseline shows substantial variance across samples driven by image-dependent convergence: simpler images with low-rank structure converge in a handful of sweeps, while images with richer high-frequency content require many more before reaching the fidelity threshold.
quotes: with substantial variance across samples driven by imagedependent convergence behavior: simpler images with low-rank structure converge in a handful of sweeps, while images with richer high-frequency content require many more before reaching the fidelity threshold.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the center-sequential ansatz with depth D=6, inference is a single forward pass through the CNN encoder with no optimization at inference time, with a median prediction latency of 0.497 ms per image, a ∼ 6580-fold speedup over per-image optimization.
quotes: In our method, the parameter prediction reduces to a single forward pass through the CNN encoder and no optimization is required at inference time.
sequential ansatz with depth D=6, the median prediction latency is 0.497 ms per image, a ∼ 6580-fold speedup over per-image optimization.
assertions.reader_inference: 3.27 s divided by 0.497 ms is about 6580. The baseline is a mean over 10 samples and the encoder figure is a median, and the latency covers predicting the parameters, not running a circuit on quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that preparing all 70 000 MNIST images by sweeping would require ∼2.65 days while their encoder completes it in ∼35 seconds, and that at industrial scale (106 images in the text layer; 1M in the figure caption) the gap widens from ∼38 days to ∼8.3 minutes.

At industrial scale (106 images), the gap widens from ∼38 days to ∼8.3 minutes
Dashed lines mark the MNIST (70K) and industrial (1M) scales.
assertions.reader_inference: These are extrapolations from 3.27 s and about 0.5 ms per image; the text does not say they were run at that scale. They agree with those per-image figures.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the approach can generate high-fidelity FRQI states with shallow circuits, and that it shifts the computational cost from online state preparation to an offline training phase, enabling new, unseen inputs to be encoded in a single forward pass.

assertions.value: The authors state in the conclusion that, compared with per-image sweeping optimization, which requires seconds per image, the trained encoder predicts circuit parameters in approximately 0.5 ms per image, a speedup of more than three orders of magnitude.

assertions.value: The authors state that reducing the cost of state preparation is a necessary step toward making quantum computing practical for data-driven applications, since quantum algorithms can only deliver useful advantages when the cost of loading and representing classical data is itself scalable.

since quantum algorithms can only deliver useful advantages when the cost of loading and representing classical data is itself scalable.
